items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, as Canada continues to deepen its trading relationship with the host country.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China -- Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, as Canada continues to deepen its trading relationship with the host country.

Asked about American concerns over Canada trading more closely with China, Carney said it is not a top priority for Trump.

“In my conversations with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China. I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all,” said Carney.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Earlier, at an APEC gathering of CEOs, Carney encouraged greater direct investment in Canadian megaprojects, including port expansions and pipelines, specifically from Asian countries and China.

While acknowledging Canada’s historic ties to the United States, Carney told delegates the world order is shifting.

“Canada is building more ambitiously and rapidly than at any time in our history,” said Carney.

“Every port and corridor we build needs a partner.”

Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday and told delegates that sanctions against Russia were a thing of the past. He also rejected the broad economic measures imposed by Canada and European countries over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Carney said Putin’s assessment of the impact of sanctions was wrong.

“You know not for the first time Vladimir Putin is lying about the situation on the ground. Sanctions are very real and they’re going to continue to increase as long as this war goes on,” said Carney.

Business leaders at the summit said Canada’s standing at APEC and across Asia is stronger than it has been in years.

“Well the tone has changed because Canada’s cool again. It’s cool again for all the right reasons,” said Goldy Hyder of the Business Council of Canada.

“They’re excited to hear the progress that Canada is making towards investment. There’s, as I said, a real star factor,” said Hyder.

items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China — Prime Minister Mark Carney secured new trade concessions from China that will benefit Canadian pork and seafood producers, while tensions over his push to attract Chinese automakers to invest in Canada continued to complicate efforts to reset relations with Beijing.

Meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit got underway, Carney heard Xi declare that China’s relationship with Canada had “fully resumed.”

  • ‘Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.?’ Trump trade adviser asks PM Carney
  • Carney and Sheinbaum meet at summit in China, as both navigate Trump’s tumult
  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The two countries announced measures to reduce tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, with pork and seafood producers among the biggest beneficiaries.

Canadian officials valued the extended tariff relief at more than $400 million, including $116 million in frozen pork cuts, $96 million in Greenland halibut, and various frozen cold-water prawns and shrimp.

“China is one of the most critical markets for pork processors and exporters,” said Kyle Larkin, president and CEO of the Canadian Meat Council, speaking to Canadian reporters in Shenzhen.

“It’s really great news for the Canadian pork industry, and more importantly for a thousand farmers and workers in Canada,” said Karan Sangfai, CEO of HyLife, one of Canada’s top pork producers.

Canadian officials were measured in describing the progress, which Carney has characterized as a “warming” of relations after years of tension, including China’s detention of Michael Spavor and Michael Kovrig.

“In total, now we are just shy of $8-billion worth of Canadian exports back into the Chinese marketplace,” said Kody Blois, parliamentary secretary to the prime minister.

He said agreements were also reached for market access to geoduck and mollusk.

“This is a major seafood market and one of the largest for us in the world, and we needed to make sure we get that market access back.”

Chinese EVs

The trade gains are part of Carney’s broader effort to diversify Canada’s economy and reduce its reliance on the United States.

Since his visit to Beijing in January 2026, the two countries have made progress on several trade issues. Canadian merchandise exports to China rose 31.4 per cent in the first half of 2026 to $21.5 billion, according to Global Affairs Canada. Crude oil shipments to China have also increased by approximately 37 per cent this year.

China has suspended additional tariffs on Canadian canola meal, peas, lobster and crab, with both countries agreeing on Nov. 4 to extend those market-access concessions through the end of 2028. China has also restored access for Canadian beef from 20 registered meat establishments.

But the push to deepen trade ties has a more contentious dimension: Carney wants Chinese automakers to consider investing in Canadian manufacturing, potentially creating opportunities for autoworkers affected by U.S. tariffs.

There was no new announcement on Chinese electric vehicles entering Canada, with the two countries maintaining the agreement reached in January 2026.

“We have the best autoworkers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. “If they are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.”

Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, responded to Carney’s comments on social media.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme. You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive,” Navarro wrote.

Carney has said any Chinese automotive investment in Canada must involve genuine domestic manufacturing, rather than simply assembling vehicles from imported Chinese parts.

“It’s not just about kit cars. There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved,” he said.

The January agreement opened the Canadian market to a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles. Canada replaced its previous 100 per cent surtax with the standard 6.1 per cent most-favoured-nation tariff, subject to an annual quota of 49,000 vehicles.

Beyond trade, the relationship remains complicated by disagreements over foreign interference, cybersecurity, human rights and national security. Carney has said closer economic engagement with China does not mean Canada is setting aside those concerns.

For Carney, the challenge is to expand Canada’s access to the Chinese market while protecting domestic industries and managing an increasingly complicated relationship with its largest trading partner, the United States.

items._ogDesc: World shares were mixed Wednesday as artificial intelligence stocks bounced back after widespread losses among the tech industry on Wall Street.
items.body:
HONG KONG — World shares were mixed Wednesday as artificial intelligence stocks bounced back after widespread losses among the tech industry on Wall Street.

U.S. futures edged higher and oil prices fell more than 1 per cent.

In early European trading, Germany’s DAX rose 0.2 per cent to 26,097.45, while France’s CAC 40 edged 0.1 per cent higher to 8,218.26. Britain’s FTSE 100 fell 0.4 per cent to 10,650.87.

U.K. inflation in October rose to 3.6 per cent, the highest level in a year, according to the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday. Rising fuel costs drove much of the increase, adding pressure on the Bank of England to raise the interest rate.

The future for the S&P 500 advanced 0.6 per cent and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.2 per cent.

In Asia, the Kospi in Seoul advanced 1.9 per cent to 5,062.92 as memory chipmaker SK Hynix surged 4.6 per cent and Samsung Electronics added 2.1 per cent.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 gained 0.3 per cent to 59,024.28. Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group climbed 3.1 per cent and testing equipment maker Advantest jumped 4.6 per cent after the lunch break.

Japan recorded a 476.5 billion yen (US$3 billion) trade deficit in October, according to government data released Wednesday. The trade deficit was up 58 per cent from a year earlier.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng fell 0.9 per cent to 23,294.75, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1 per cent lower to 3,587.83.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.7 per cent to 8,821.80.

Taiwan’s Taiex moved 0.1 per cent higher.

India’s Sensex declined 0.8 per cent.

Investors will be watching the APEC summit beginning Wednesday in Shenzhen, China, where world leaders gather to discuss regional trade and economic cooperation.

The Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic, Chinese President Xi Jinping told business executives on the sidelines of the summit.

Trade relations will be a focus as U.S. President Donald Trump and Xi are set to meet for the third time this year.

On Tuesday, the S&P 500 sank 1 per cent and at one point was on track for its first back-to-back losses of at least 1.5 per cent since March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 848 points, or 1.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.7 per cent.

The center of the action was again Nvidia, which resumed its whipsaw moves. After flipping between modest gains and losses in the morning, it dropped as much as 3.7 per cent before trimming the loss down to 0.4 per cent.

The swings came ahead of the chip company’s latest earnings report, which arrived after trading ended for the day and once again came in above analysts’ expectations. It was Nvidia’s first earnings report since interim CEO Colette Kress took over for Jensen Huang.

The pressure is on Kress and Nvidia to show whether the company’s tremendous growth can continue following the stunning resignation of one of AI’s strongest influencers. Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance.

Huang said on the X social-media network Tuesday that he would come back as CEO if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.”

AI-related stocks have been shaky for months because of a rolling chain of worries. At first, it was concerned that AI stock prices had broadly shot too high in their frenzy. Then it was worried that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund further growth.

Most of Wall Street was weak Tuesday, as 17 out of every 20 stocks within the index fell.

The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15 per cent Tuesday morning from 5.12 per cent late Monday before later pulling back to 5.10 per cent.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 0.8 per cent to $93.14. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.

In other dealings Wednesday, the price of Brent crude, the international standard, was 1.6 per cent down to $91.67 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped 2.1 per cent to $84.19 per barrel.

The U.S. dollar slid to 159.22 Japanese yen from 159.40 yen. The euro fell to $1.0968 from $1.0994.

Elaine Lai, The Associated Press

items.title: Can advocates elected to Toronto council help fix housing and homelessness crisis?
items.description: Toronto’s newly elected council includes several prominent tenant and housing rights activists and advocates for the city’s homeless population who say they will bring the kind of first-hand outreach experience to the table that council needs.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A man sleeps on the street in Toronto, on Friday, March 11, 2022. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Chris Young]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Chris Young</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Toronto’s newly elected council includes several prominent tenant and housing rights activists and advocates for the city’s homeless population who say they will bring the kind of first-hand outreach experience to the table that council needs.
items.body:
TORONTO — Toronto’s newly elected council includes several prominent tenant and housing rights activists and advocates for the city’s homeless population who say they will bring the kind of first-hand outreach experience to the table that council needs.

While some observers aren’t sure that advocates-turned-councillors can significantly change the direction of Toronto’s housing and homelessness policies, the rookie members say they have the political will to use their advocacy expertise to help address the city’s affordability crisis.

Diana Chan McNally, a longtime outreach worker who is now representing Parkdale-High Park in the city’s west end, said while she has a list of other priorities, such as improving public transit and ensuring the waterfront remains accessible and environmentally sound in her ward, she is committed to do what she did as an advocate in her new municipal decision-making role.

“I worked for 12 years with people on the streets and you learn very quickly that (homelessness) has nothing to do with the individual and it has everything to do with things like affordability, access to health care,” she said.

“So, (I’m) very interested in continuing this work, very interested in making sure that we have a platform and pathway, essentially, for people to have their voice heard and also for policies to actually reflect their needs.”

The current term of the housing rights advisory committee, established by city council in 2023, is ending this month and McNally, who was a member of the committee, said she is hoping to bring it back.

“I think this is a great space in which we can continue to push forward, ensuring that people’s rights, for those who are out on the street who don’t own property, are actually taken care of,” she said.

Chiara Padovani, a tenants’ organizer, is another well-known activist who secured a victory after unseating longtime councillor Frances Nunziata in York South-Weston in last month’s municipal election. She said that she will also continue advocating for tenants.

Cristine de Clercy, a political scientist who teaches at Trent University, said it is easier for activists to criticize lawmakers and offer policy ideas as outsiders. Once they become part of the government, they need to learn to compromise and navigate internal dynamics to successfully work on their priorities, she said.

“The new councillors, it’s inevitably the case that because now they’re inside of machinery of government, they don’t have free rein to simply advocate willy-nilly for whatever policy,” she said.

McNally said she is aware that being a politician and being an advocate are two different roles and she needs to be pragmatic, but she is certain she won’t compromise her core progressive values, including housing rights.

“My goal is to make sure that, you know, people who used to be my colleagues are holding my feet to the fire, that the public is ensuring that I stay true to my own values,” she said.

Toronto’s homelessness and housing affordability crises have always been pressing issues at city hall in recent decades and they’ve escalated since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Officials at different levels of government have been discussing the problem, providing funding and taking actions, but critics have often said too little is done to help homeless people and struggling tenants in Canada’s largest city.

Padovani was among the advocates who helped tenants organize several rent strikes against what she called unfair landlords.

She said road safety and flood protection are two major issues in her ward that she will focus on, but she will also always fight for tenants’ rights.

“Tenant voices have been ignored by … so many in the city government,” she said. “And I’m really looking forward to making sure that if you’re a slumlord in my community, I’m going to be taking you to task and I’ll be holding you accountable.”

As a councillor, she said she will make sure the city enforces building standards more vigorously.

“What I want to do is start passing bylaws at the City of Toronto that puts the onus on the city to protect tenant rights and alleviate some of the pressure on tenants,” she said.

Padovani said she understands that residential tenancy rights are primarily governed by the province, but that doesn’t mean the city can’t do anything to protect renters against abusive landlords.

She praised Mayor Olivia Chow for leading the effort to pass the rental renovation licence bylaw, which makes renovictions — a tactic critics say is used by landlords to evade rent control and increase rent prices — more difficult.

Padovani said she will push council to pass a similar bylaw against rent increases above the provincial guideline, known as AGI, which have sparked several rent strikes in Toronto in recent years.

“I have a feeling this is going to be something that a lot of my colleagues are going to be interested in, in order to start to think creatively about how to make life more affordable for the half of the city that rent their home,” she said.

Nearly half of Toronto’s population rents their homes. That number is over 70 per cent in the densely populated Toronto Centre, according to Curran Stikuts, the ward’s new councillor who said the area is also home to many homeless shelters and overnight respite centres.

Stikuts, an advocate with more than 15 years of experience working with renters and marginalized communities in the area, including queer youth who are homeless, campaigned on housing affordability and was elected over incumbent Chris Moise.

Stikuts said fighting against renovictions and ensuring that buildings are kept up to standards and the city provides support for tenants are among the issues he wants to tackle on council. He said working with homeless people has taught him that “four walls and a roof” isn’t enough to solve the problem.

“It’s really, I think, about focusing on the ways in which we’re building not just the units and spaces, but the levels of supports and wraparound care that we need to make people stable and then get back on their feet,” he said.

Pointing to a report from the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario, Toronto said homelessness in Toronto has deceased by over eight per cent, while increasing by nearly 18 per cent provincewide, between 2022 and 2025.

Despite the progress, the city said it is still in a state of “homelessness emergency” caused by unaffordable housing, inadequate income support and unmet health needs.

The recently tabled federal budget includes nearly $30 billion toward the government’s goal to end homelessness across the country over the next decade, and Stikuts said while he was encouraged by the news, he would love to see some of that money flow to Toronto quicker to get “shovels in the ground.”

Greg Cook, an outreach team lead at Sanctuary Ministries of Toronto, said improving living conditions for homeless people hasn’t been a top priority for Chow during her first term.

“The city has said it’s a crisis, but they’re not treating it as such,” he said.

The mayor’s office, however, said she has been working hard to build more shelters and supportive housing, and invest in eviction prevention programs aimed at curbing homelessness.

It said the city has moved 15,000 people from shelters and encampments into permanent housing, including 4,700 people in 2025.

“Over the past two years, homelessness in Toronto declined, despite growing across the province. There is more work to do and the mayor has been committed to addressing it,” Chow’s spokesperson Braman Thillainathan wrote in a statement.

Cook said even though a progressive-leaning council has an opportunity to make some progress, they can’t do it alone.

“It will require a significant kind of community pressure, and I think there might be some councillors who are more willing to kind of stick their neck out and speak on behalf of people who are poor,” he said.

Asked if community advocates who are joining council for the first time could serve as allies for the homeless community in municipal government, Cook said: “I wouldn’t probably go that far. I think politicians are going to do what is going to keep them in power.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 18, 2026.

Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

items.title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
items.description: After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A billboard announcing the release of the "Grand Theft Auto VI" video game is displayed near Times Square, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Yuki Iwamura</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.
items.body:
LOS ANGELES — After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.

“Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.

The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, meaning players in Asia and other regions will begin entering the game hours before its U.S. release.

New Zealand will be among the first countries where players can access the game and internet providers there are preparing for a surge in downloads as midnight arrives.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”

The company expects about 35 petabytes of additional traffic across its network, which Rodgers called “enormous.”

The expectations are enormous, too.

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide, while “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and reached US$1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Rockstar is returning to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following a game that became one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.

Game returns to Vice City after 13 years

At the centre of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.

Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.

Their relationship marks one of the biggest departures from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.

Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, stretching beyond Vice City into beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities. They flew over the Everglades and researched the area’s history and architecture.

Miami embraces its fictional alter ego

Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.

Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.

The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.

Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.

In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.

Years of hype arrive at launch day

Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.

The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.

“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.

Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.

For “GTA VI,” Rockstar commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing. A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.

What players will find next

Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.

The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.

Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.

Those answers will begin emerging first from players in Asia and Europe as midnight arrives in their regions, followed by North America hours later.

Jonathan Landrum Jr., The Associated Press

Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
items.body:
SHENZHEN, China — U.S. President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.

The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.

“It’s fine,” Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”

But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the spectre that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.

So at the start of the second day of Trump’s trip, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump’s behalf. He told reporters there was “zero” evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.

“Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you’ve identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption,” said Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser.

Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image

Xi paid Trump a special honour by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.

The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.

Trump has signalled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It’s a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.

The White House said that Trump would have two separate meetings on Wednesday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.

On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia’s invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.

Before the trip, Trump’s aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.

“I think it’s very close to getting it done,” Trump said. “We’re going to have a good meeting on that.”

Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. But neither option had been added to his official schedule.

Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos

Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.

Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for “working very hard.”

Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.

“Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes,” Trump said. “I love what you’ve done here.”

He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached.

Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines’ current president.

Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 “People Power” uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines’ strongman leader.

Trump called her “always the most beautiful” and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.

What’s on the agenda for Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin

The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America’s largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.

His tariffs that were intended to curb China’s trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.

Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.

The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.

Trump’s close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.

When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China’s access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”

Price reported from Manila, Philippines. AP writers Darlene Superville in Washington and Jim Gomez in Manila contributed to this report.

Josh Boak And Michelle L. Price, The Associated Press

items.body:
One of Canada’s most well-known charitable organizations says it’s changing its name.

March of Dimes Canada will now be known as Disability Can, the charity says in a press release.

The charity, which provides services and programs to people living with disabilities, says the name change better reflects how the organization has evolved over the past 75 years.

The charity says in a press release that the new name will also make it easier for people to find the programs and services they need.

March of Dimes Canada was founded in 1951 as a response to the threat of polio, raising funds for vaccine research and helping people who contracted the virus.

Today the charity has more than 2,500 employees and 550 volunteers who serve more than 30,000 people each year, the organization says.

Len Baker, president and CEO of Disability Can, says the decision to change the name came directly from listening to people with disabilities.

“It reflects a modern understanding of disability, clearly says who we are and what we do, and expresses a truth we’ve always known: disability doesn’t limit what people can achieve — barriers do,” Baker said in a statement.

The original name was a reference to a campaign by mothers to raise funds for polio causes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

items.title: Carney tells Pacific Rim businesses that China’s growth a model for Canada
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney is meeting with leaders from across the Pacific Rim at a summit in China’s tech hub Shenzhen, and is set to address reporters overnight.

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney is meeting with leaders from across the Pacific Rim at a summit in China’s tech hub Shenzhen, and is set to address reporters overnight.
items.body:
SHENZHEN -- Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canadians should learn from China’s breakneck economic growth, while insisting Ottawa has the right guardrails on expanding trade with Beijing to limit interference and U.S. blowback.

“We try to be clear with them. There are opportunities to unleash investment, and there are not in other parts of our economy,” Carney said in French at a news conference in Shenzhen, China.

Carney is attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, where he also said the development of the city of Shenzhen -- from a fishing village to a high-tech mega city -- shows what can be achieved by cutting red tape and building fast.

The prime minister’s visit started with an announcement that Canada would drop certain restrictions on importing Chinese steel and aluminum in exchange for more market access for Canadian pork and other agricultural products.

The announcement also included a partnership on artificial intelligence -- though Carney previously said that was among three sectors off-limits to Chinese investment in Canada, along with critical minerals and defence industries.

Carney said discussions with China have focused more on how to safeguard against economic and biosecurity risks.

“The absence of any global governance around AI is an enormous risk,” Carney said. “I took the opportunity in the discussions with President Xi yesterday to share our views on a model for how this governance can be developed.”

Carney said Canada would shape its trade based on shared interests, giving the example of the European Union having press freedoms while other areas don’t. “The calibration depends on the values that we share with countries,” he said in French.

He said more market access to China benefits various regions of Canada, such as fishers and farmers, “but relative to many other countries, our trade with China is quite modest -- and the breadth of it is quite modest,” he said.

Carney said there are steps to how Canada recalibrates its relations with China, which follows a diplomatic crisis in 2018 and repeated concerns about foreign interference, which Beijing has denied.

“We’ve pursued a stabilization of the relationship first and a gradual opening of the relationship,” the prime minister said.

Carney’s recent agreements with China on trade raised the ire of those close to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Peter Navarro, the president’s trade adviser, has said it was “offensive in the extreme” for Carney to be “threatening to play China off the U.S.”

The prime minister said Canadian trade with China does not involve cutting-edge technology as does American trade with Beijing.

Earlier Wednesday, Carney said Ottawa was trying to expedite major projects while working with countries such as China to limit its dependence on countries like the United States.

“I’ll be clear: these partnerships remain vital, but Canada is also a Pacific nation,” he told the CEO summit at APEC.

“The next chapter of Canada’s transformation will be written with partners in this region.”

His remarks come months after the prime minister intensely focused on deepening ties with Europe. In June, he said a “new world order” would be built from Europe and pursuing some sort of “associate membership” in the European Union.

Speaking on the sidelines of the CEO summit, analysts said Carney should pursue the strengths of each continent.

“When it comes to Europe (it’s) defence, AI,” said Goldy Hyder, CEO of the Business Council of Canada.

“Asia in particular needs our energy, needs our food. And so the opportunities to do both are very much available for Canada, and that’s where growth is going to come from.”

Jeff Nankivell, head of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, said it was encouraging that Carney had spent the week at summits in China, Cambodia and the Philippines.

“It’s been very consequential,” he said. He added that it’s not clear whether Canadians would take up opportunities in the region.

“Canadians are capable of being fast. We’re also capable, as we’ve seen, of getting in our own way.”

The prime minister told reporters that he has had “open, frank conversations” with Xi on matters that Carney has chosen to not make a focus of his public comments.

“Issues of human rights, issues of foreign interference, issues of transnational crime, narcotics trade -- we raise them with our counterparts, including part of my discussions with President Xi.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Following public scrutiny over automaker Stellantis’ sale of its Brampton, Ont. plant, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to meet with the company once again on Friday, her office tells CTV News.
items.body:
OTTAWA – Following public scrutiny over automaker Stellantis’ sale of its Brampton, Ont. plant, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is set to meet with the company once again on Friday, her office tells CTV News.

According to Joly’s press secretary Mathis Denis, the meeting will be with Stellantis Global CEO Antonio Filosa, along with officials from the Ontario government and the union Unifor in Toronto.

The potentially high-stakes meeting comes as the federal government faces questions over its involvement in and knowledge of the plant sale prior to the announcement last week.

After months of speculation, Stellantis announced its plan to sell its Brampton plant — which has been idled since 2023 — to Roshel, a Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer. More than 2,200 workers have been on lay-off pay.

The federal government initially expressed outrage at the announcement of the sale, and pledged to hold the company accountable, with Prime Minister Mark Carney calling the move a “betrayal,” and Joly threatening to sue Stellantis if it sells the plant. Carney a day later called the sale a “partial solution.”

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Multiple sources, however, have told CTV News that senior officials within both the Prime Minister’s Office and Joly’s office were aware of the proposed sale for months, and behind the scenes, did not stand in the way of it advancing.

Lobby records also show high-level meetings between government officials and Stellantis and Roshel in the months leading up to the sale.

Late last week, however, despite threatening to sue, Joly said the federal government would also offer Stellantis an “aggressive package” to prevent the sale, and she did not rule out more taxpayer money going to the company.

“If it’s to save the plant, we would be actually doing what we’ve done with Ford, what we’ve done with Honda, and what we’ve done with Toyota, and what we’re willing to do with all automakers and auto suppliers that are affected by the tariffs,” Joly said in an interview with CTV Question Period on Sunday.

In 2022, the federal government committed up to $529 million to Stellantis to retool both its plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont. Records show $222 million had been paid out as of March 2025. Stellantis has offered to pay back $24 million to the federal government.

CTV News has reached out to Stellantis for comment on Friday’s meeting.

With files from CTV News’ Vassy Kapelos, Marieke Walsh and Spencer Van Dyk

items._ogDesc: October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday. Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.
items.body:
October home sales crept up slightly from the previous month but were still down more than 10 per cent from a year ago, the Canadian Real Estate Association said in its latest report Tuesday.

Home sales last month totalled 37,827, down 10.6 per cent from October 2025. But on a seasonally adjusted basis, activity edged up 0.3 per cent compared with September.

“Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” Garry Bhaura, CREA's chair, said in a news release.

“With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027."

The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month — the first hike in more than three years — to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation.

The move prompted Canada's big banks to raise their benchmark prime rates, pushing the amount charged on variable rate mortgages higher.

A summary of deliberations released earlier this month by the central bank also suggested its governing council thinks it might need to raise rates further, but will proceed carefully.

Michael Davenport, senior economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a report Tuesday that Canada's resale housing market had a quiet October and is heading into "hibernation" for the winter.

"Rising mortgage rates, a soft labour market and elevated job insecurity from the trade war with the United States will likely cause housing demand to weaken in the near term, pushing home sales and prices modestly lower before a tepid recovery gets underway next spring," he wrote.

"We don’t expect the recent softness in the housing market to deter the (Bank of Canada) from hiking ... to 2.75 per cent in December."

Meanwhile, CREA said the national average sale price in October ticked down 1.6 per cent from a year ago to $678,584.

New listings fell 5.5 per cent to 75,814, but on a seasonally adjusted basis, were up 0.8 per cent from the month before and outpaced sales activity.

CREA said there were about 197,000 properties listed for sale on all Canadian MLS systems at the end of October, up slightly from the long-term average of 190,000.

It said there were five months of inventory on a national basis at the end of October, up slightly from the summer.

Cailey Heaps, CEO at Heaps Estrin Real Estate Team in Toronto, said deals are coming together when sellers have realistic expectations about pricing and buyers are willing to act.

The segment that's been the most challenging has been for properties that are "family homes" to be lived in long-term.

"Those people are currently housed, so they don't feel any pressure to act. They want to take a bit of a wait-and-see approach," she said.

"The first-time buyer market is very active — incredibly active."

Heaps is expecting a "fairly flat" market through the winter as concern over job security and tariffs weigh on confidence.

"And then I do think that spring will start to see an uptick, not only in pricing but also in volume."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate’s has one of the largest corrections in history and it’s still going, as buyers balked at this price level in October.
items.body:
Canadian real estate has made one of the sharpest corrections on record, and it’s still going. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows prices fell further in October. Weak demand and lofty inventory suggest that buyers are still balking at this level. Over 4 years in a correction have only rolled back 13 months of 2020’s low rate, speculative boom.

Canada’s Housing Correction Reversed 13 Months of Gains

The price of a typical home across Canada.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.3% (-$2.1k) to $649.9k in October, 3.1% (-$20.7k) lower than last year. Prices are now 22.8% (-$191.6k) lower than the March 2022 peak, and sit just a little higher than they were back in February 2021. Nearly half a decade of correcting, and most Canadians still couldn’t afford to buy, even if they wanted to.

Canadian Home Sales Fall, Remain Historically Weak

Canadian home sales on the MLS in October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

There was an abrupt drop in home sales last month. Only 37.8k homes were sold in October, 10.6% fewer than last year and marks a 3-year low. That doesn’t sound bad, but excluding the slowdown since 2022, this level was last seen in 2012. Home sales are better than they were at the start of the downturn, but are still hovering around levels seen in the wake of the global financial crisis.

Canadian Home Sellers Still Flooding The Market

New listings of homes for sale on the Canadian MLS, October.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The inventory side weakened too—just not as much as it did when it comes to home sales. CREA reported 75.8k new listings in October, 5.5% lower than last year, and just a smidge under October 2024. This may be a 3-year low, but October’s new listings have never been this strong before 2020.

A sharper drop in sales left the sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) at 49.9% in October, 2.8 points below last year. The ratio is technically in balanced territory, but this time of year tends to see sellers pull back. The SNLR doesn’t show a buyer’s market, but October hasn’t seen the ratio this low since 2008. In fact, that’s the only October to come in lower in the past three decades.

When does this market downturn end? This is one of the sharpest downturns on record, yet not much progress has been made. The market’s been like a slow-moving car crash, spending over 4 years rolling back just 13 months of gains. Home prices in Canada have always moved fast, but from 2015 to 2022 was another story. Taxpayer-backed incentives helped to grow prices much faster than incomes and credit capacity. The inefficiencies didn’t build up overnight, and they won’t correct overnight either.

items.content: <p>Daniele Grechi, a partner at the firm, tells CMP why supporting this year’s crop of commercial brokers is more important than ever</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639294998909890808.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Daniele Grechi, a partner at the firm, tells CMP why supporting this year’s crop of commercial brokers is more important than ever
items.body:
With just days remaining until one of the most anticipated events in Canada’s mortgage industry calendar, Excellence Awardees and their teams are gearing up for what’s sure to be an unforgettable night at the Canadian Mortgage Awards at Rebel Toronto (November 25).

The event – now entering its 20th year – wouldn’t be the same without the involvement of the award sponsors, who play a crucial role in supporting and recognizing the best and brightest in the mortgage industry.

Toronto real estate law firm Grechi Carter Professional Corporation will present the award for Broker of the Year – Commercial next week, and Daniele Grechi (pictured top), a partner at the firm, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that supporting the event marks a natural extension of the company’s push into the lending community.

“While Grechi Carter is a full-service real estate law firm, at our core we’re a lending firm,” he said. “Lending represents the majority of our business, extending even to our litigation department, which specializes in mortgage enforcement.”

“As a firm, we’ve made it a priority to deepen our involvement in the lending community, and we view the Canadian Mortgage Awards as the pinnacle of industry recognition.”

The company has developed a strong presence in private lending and among mortgage investment corporations (MICs), which pool investor capital to fund mortgages. Grechi said he views commercial lending as the next frontier.

“Having established a strong presence in the private lending and MIC sectors, we’re particularly excited to broaden our relationships within the commercial lending space,” he said. “Supporting these awards is a natural extension of that commitment.”

Celebrating top performers in an eventful market

The CMAs have taken place during years of market turbulence before – from the financial crash to the COVID-era volatility – and the 2026 event arrives against a backdrop of a cooling mortgage market, affordability struggles, and rising interest rates.

Grechi acknowledged the challenging market, but sounded an optimistic tone on what’s in store. “The past few years have been exceptionally challenging for the mortgage and real estate industries,” he said. “However, we are optimistic that we’re at or near the bottom of this cycle and that better days are ahead.”

Excellence Awardees have been named across more than 20 different categories at this year’s CMAs, with final winners to be announced at the glitzy ceremony next Wednesday.

For Grechi, downturns separate the strongest operators from the rest, and those who continue to navigate the current market challenges are likely to succeed in the long run.

“Periods like these tend to distinguish the most resilient, adaptable and capable professionals in our industry,” he said. “As the market recovers, we believe those who have weathered this storm will be particularly well positioned to capitalize on the opportunities ahead. That makes recognizing excellence in our industry all the more meaningful this year.”

How Grechi Carter has approached 2026

Setting up for success for Grechi Carter in the present market has meant continuing to spend even while the market has been weak, Grechi said. “We’ve continued to invest in our people, expertise and technology throughout this market cycle,” he said.

“In particular, we have developed tailored AI-driven processes to enhance quality control, efficiency and consistency, with the objective of delivering the highest standard of legal service to our lending partners. We believe these investments position us well for the next cycle of growth.”

Seven brokers are shortlisted for the Commercial Broker award: Ahmed Hatata of Green Mortgage Solutions Inc., Alexander Durand of Mcommercial, Jason McNeill of 4Capital Mortgages, Jean Luc Dion of Multi-Prêts Commercial, Jonathan Gagnon of Orbis Mortgage Group, Peter Quinn of Multi-Prêts Commercial, and Stephen Thomas of Mortgage Alliance HALO Mortgage Advisory.

Grechi paid tribute to the industry members who have gone above and beyond for clients in a difficult time for many commercial borrowers. “Those who have successfully navigated this environment have demonstrated tremendous resourcefulness and commitment to their businesses and clients,” he said.

items.title: Canadian Home Sales Inch Up In October As Interest Rates Climb
items.description:
The Canadian housing market barely moved in October, which is a better result than many forecasters expected heading into fall. Home sales on Canadian MLS® Systems rose 0.3% from September, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

October also brought a rate hike from the Bank of Canada. CREA doesn’t expect it to turn into a repeat of 2022.

“In a widely expected move, the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate at its October 28 announcement with the goal of tamping down Canadians’ concerns about creeping inflation stemming from higher energy costs,” said Shaun Cathcart, CREA’s Senior Economist. “That said, with the Bank’s preferred inflation measures still very well behaved, this is unlikely to be a repeat of the 2022 tightening cycle. Rather, it is more likely to be of the mild to moderate variety, although that distinction does carry extra weight in times of stretched affordability.”

So far, buyers haven’t pulled back much. “Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” said Garry Bhaura, CREA Chair.

The year-over-year comparison is weaker. Actual (not seasonally adjusted) sales were 10.6% lower than in October 2025.

New listings grew 0.8% month-over-month. Listings rose a little faster than sales did, so the national sales-to-new listings ratio slipped to 48.7% from 49% in September. That’s under the long-term average of 54.7%, but still within the 45% to 65% band CREA associates with a balanced market.

There were roughly 197,000 properties listed for sale nationwide at the end of October, slightly above the long-term average of 190,000. At this point in the year, inventory has ranged from 100,000 listings in fall 2021, when the COVID-19 housing boom was at its peak, to 250,000 a little over a decade ago.

Measured in time, the market had five months of inventory at the end of October. That’s up slightly from the summer and exactly in line with the long-term average. By CREA’s measure, a seller’s market sits below 3.6 months and a buyer’s market sits above 6.4 months.

On prices, the National Composite MLS® Home Price Index (HPI) rose 0.1% from September. CREA said that gain could reasonably be called flat, or the biggest monthly increase in two years.

On an annual basis, the non-seasonally adjusted HPI was 3.1% below October 2025. That’s a smaller drop than September’s and smaller than most of the readings so far in 2026.

The non-seasonally adjusted national average home price came in at $678,584, which is 1.6% lower than a year earlier.

The slow season is next. “With the market moving into its traditionally quieter months, now is a great time to shift into planning mode for 2027,” said Bhaura.

CREA will release its next set of statistics on Tuesday, December 15, 2026.

items.title: How AI is making brokers more powerful
items.description: Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat
items.content: <p>Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639305467499655022.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Top broker on why artificial intelligence is an invaluable tool for brokers – not a threat
items.body:
The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in the mortgage sector has led t plenty of questions about how the role of mortgage brokers will evolve – but as Streetwise Mortgages founder and Wisely AI co-founder Dalia Barsoum told us at MortgageFest Canada, there are huge opportunities for brokers to utilize the technology to grow and boost their business.

[00:00] This is making us more powerful brokers. AI still needs human judgment. What's effective is to have it do certain things within boundaries but oversee it, train it, and that's where the human touch comes in.

[00:26] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So next up we are joined by Dalia Barsoum who we all know as the founder of Streetwise Mortgages, also coming with a new role this year, co-founder of Wisely AI, which I'm really excited to talk to you about because AI, as we all know, has been a big topic in the industry over the past couple of years. Tell us about Wisely AI. How did the idea come about and what are you guys up to?

[00:49] Dalia Barsoum: So as you know, the market in Ontario and BC shifted, and as a business our revenue got hit and our volume got hit. We had to reinvent ourselves to run leaner so that we can sustain because we don't know how long the runway is, and also to be able to handle more volume once things recover without having to add back our old cost base.

[01:20] That's how the idea started. My co-founder is an engineer and an AI-certified tech geek, and he was basically the one that said, "You know what? Let's find better ways to support the brokerage." That's how the idea came about. How can we integrate AI in our workflow in a smart way, safe way, to be able to handle the volume without adding the cost base and enhance client experience.

[01:49] Fergal McAlinden: It's interesting that you have your eye on when things pick up, which we're hoping will be in the next couple of years. How will the technology that you're developing help brokers once that new wave comes about?

[01:59] Dalia Barsoum: Right now we're integrating AI along the mortgage life cycle, the journey. So from intake to close and nurture, there are opportunities, and every broker is different.

[02:12] For us, we've used AI, we call them AI minions right now. We've used them to enhance our marketing, increase our lead generation, enhance our conversion. We use them to review documents and save time on that front. We also use them to answer the phone and intake from all of our social media channels.

[02:38] The one that we rolled out to the market is the compliance assistant. It's not going to say, "Hey, I've done compliance for you." But it's going to assist you as a principal broker in the process, reducing your time from 40 minutes to 2 minutes and making sure it's surfacing things that you don't see as a human, which we've come across. That's basically what we're doing right now, and we're rolling these minions to the industry, starting with the compliance assistant.

[03:07] Fergal McAlinden: Sounds great. We all remember whenever ChatGPT and other LLMs first gained popularity and there was all this talk about existential threats to certain professions and things like that. I think most people thought about the mortgage industry that it would be a supplement and it would help. It wasn't going to replace brokers. This, to me, seems evidence of that. It's not replacing brokers, it's helping them.

[03:28] Dalia Barsoum: One hundred percent. This is making us more powerful brokers. It's like having an assistant that saves you time, makes you stronger, faster, smarter, to free up your time to focus on what you came to this industry to do, which is serving more people and getting your time back to have a fulfilling business that can support you and your family the way you envisioned.

[03:53] AI still needs human judgment. You cannot have AI run the show for you. What's effective is to have it do certain things within boundaries, but oversee it, train it, and that's where the human touch comes in. Then you can focus on what you're really good at that machines cannot replace.

[04:13] Fergal McAlinden: Absolutely. Let's talk a little bit about the current market. We all know that there are challenges for a lot of borrowers, challenges for a lot of clients. What type of market have you been seeing this year and is it different to what we saw in 2025?

[04:25] Dalia Barsoum: So, we're still seeing pain in this market. Let me put it this way. Obviously when the rates went up, things started to shift and it's been a couple of years now. We're still seeing pain with debt levels, with values.

[04:44] Having said that, and I tell everybody, in every obstacle there is an opportunity. If we know what problems to solve for in this environment and there are people who need our help, then we're going to be able to reach out to new types of clients and solve new problems. We're starting to do that in our brokerage and it did open up doors for us because I think sometimes we get comfortable doing the same thing over and over and over.

[05:11] I'm still seeing pain. I recently published a book actually called The Rebound Advantage that talks about financial setbacks, just because we're still seeing quite a bit of that. That's an opportunity for brokers to help clients who are in different pain situations.

[05:28] But also, here's the thing. I find that the media brushes everything with the same brush and obviously tries to magnify the negative. I can tell you that in this market there are clients that are growing without pain and investing and they're still doing well. So the question for us brokers: how can we reach the growing trends in this economy and serve them and solve a problem?

[05:53] Fergal McAlinden: I think maybe at CMP we're a little bit more attuned to it because we cover the mortgage and real estate sectors more than others maybe. But what we always hear is that the housing market downturn has regional differences. Maybe some parts of the country aren't doing well but others are flourishing.

[06:09] Dalia Barsoum: Of course. Yes. I'm talking Ontario primarily.

[06:11] Fergal McAlinden: For sure. But even within Ontario, there are certain pockets that are doing very well. Certain types of property, even within the condo sector. So-called dog crates aren't doing well, but others are actually flourishing. It's a nuanced picture, I think.

[06:25] Dalia Barsoum: One hundred percent. On that note, for example, I'm seeing clients that are doing well in cottage country, believe it or not, but mass market in some pockets is not doing well. So again, you have to deconstruct and look for pockets of growth and opportunity. Even in an environment like this, you will find them. If you solve the problem, that's how you grow your volume and continue to progress, even though the big picture, when you zoom out, seems to be dark and ugly.

[06:59] Fergal McAlinden: No, that's the right attitude for sure. Looking forward to seeing what's next from Wisely AI. Anything that you're focusing on for the next few months or any trends you have your eye on?

[07:07] Dalia Barsoum: So just the focus is, again, The Rebound Advantage, the book that I put out. It's not just for clients. It's for me to share with everybody in the industry that has experienced a financial setback in their business, but also as a tool to help their clients.

[07:22] I am looking forward to sharing more of that. And then on the Wisely AI front, just putting an AI compliance support minion in the hands of those who need it. We're bringing more minions to the table in 2027 on other fronts of the mortgage journey. So that's the focus.

[07:37] Fergal McAlinden: Perfect. Well, I always appreciate your time. Pleasure to talk to you. Best of luck.

[07:41] Dalia Barsoum: Thank you very much. Thank you.

items.title: Insider: Ontario And Quebec Are Running Opposite Housing Experiments
items.description:
I have lost count of how many times I have heard that Toronto and Vancouver are a special case. Too expensive, too much debt, a local hangover. October is getting in the way of that story.

In CREA's residential numbers, Greater Toronto sales were down 7.9% from last October. Greater Vancouver was down 10.7%. Calgary was down 12.8%. Ottawa was down 10.8%. Montreal was down 17.6%. The country was down 10.6%. If those two cities were still a quarantine zone, the others would not be on that list.

Prices have not followed in every market, and that is the part worth sitting with. Calgary's benchmark was unchanged at $569,300. Montreal's was still up 1.4%, to $591,400. Ottawa was only down 1.5%. Toronto is down 4.4% on the year and 13.7% over three years. Vancouver is down 5.2%. Volume goes first. Price lags. Then the "isolated incident" starts to look like a leading indicator.

Two provinces, opposite directions

That national demand story sits on top of a supply split I still think is the more interesting chart in this release. Ontario recorded 33,510 new residential listings in October, 8.8% fewer than a year ago, against 14,053 sales, down 8.7%. Quebec went the other way on supply: 13,864 new listings, up 6.2%, against 7,451 sales, down 12.6%. Ontario's new listings have run below year-ago levels for essentially all of 2026. Quebec's have run above.

Chart: New listings, year-over-year %, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

The Greater Toronto benchmark is $928,800, down 4.4% year over year. Mississauga is down 8.5%. Quebec CMA is up 5.1%, and 33.6% over three years. Ontario is tightening the shelf and still losing price. Quebec is adding listings and still gaining some.

Toronto tightened by subtraction

Through the first ten months of 2026, the Greater Toronto Area logged 145,345 new listings, 14.7% fewer than the same period last year. Sales were 52,694, down only 1.8%. The year-to-date sales-to-new-listings ratio rose to 36.3% from 31.5%.

That "improvement" came from sellers stepping back. Buyers did not arrive. Even after a year of withdrawals, Toronto's seasonally adjusted ratio was 39.1% in October, still under the 45% floor of CREA's balanced range.

Chart: Sales-to-new-listings ratio, seasonally adjusted. Toronto vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

Montreal moved the other way. Year-to-date new listings rose 6.3% to 69,458 while sales fell 8.7% to 37,091, pulling the ratio down to 53.4% from 62.2%. Montreal is loosening from a seller's market toward balance. Toronto is crawling up from a buyer's market by shrinking the choice set.

Chart: Months of inventory, seasonally adjusted. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

I would not tell a Quebec builder the Ontario correction has landed in Montreal prices. I also would not tell them demand is insulated. Montreal sales were down 17.6% in October, in a market where prices are still rising. Some of that is rates. Montreal's benchmark sits about $337,000 below Toronto's, so a hike bites less than it does on a GTA loan. Some of it, in my view, is confidence and equity travelling. When Toronto and Vancouver values fall, owners feel poorer. They spend less and they move less. Investors who hold product in more than one city get careful. Lenders do too. I cannot show you a contagion index. I can show you volumes weakening in places that were supposed to be fine.

The pipeline tells the longer story

Resale listings are this month's supply. Housing starts are the supply of 2029 and 2030.

From January through September 2026, Ontario's housing starts averaged a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 61,200, according to CMHC data compiled on Homies stats. Quebec averaged about 60,100. Ontario's pace is down 5.7% from the same months of 2025. Quebec's is up 1.8%.

Those two numbers are nearly identical. The provinces are not. Statistics Canada estimates Ontario's population at about 16.26 million and Quebec's at about 9.07 million as of July 2026. Per 1,000 residents, Quebec is starting homes at an annualized pace of roughly 6.6. Ontario is at roughly 3.8.

Chart: Housing starts, seasonally adjusted annual rate, Ontario vs Quebec, indexed to January 2022. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Ontario's resale market is reaching balance by holding product back. Its development pipeline is doing the same thing. If the demand softness in Toronto is a leading indicator rather than a local mess, that is a problem for anyone underwriting 2028 absorption in the rest of the country.

The condo collapse is a resale problem first

Nationally, condo starts from January through September totalled 25,719, down 34.8% from 39,446 in the same months of 2025. Purpose-built rental starts rose 8.6% to 90,623.

Chart: Condo vs rental housing starts, Canada, indexed to January 2023. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CMHC via Statistics Canada.

Presale condo projects need buyers willing to pay tomorrow's price today, and lenders need those presales before construction financing flows. When the GTA resale benchmark is down 13.7% over three years, the comparable undercuts the presale, the presales do not get sold, and the project does not start.

A rate hike makes that worse. The Bank of Canada raised the overnight rate to 2.50% from 2.25% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023. Then the five-year Canada bond, the thing lenders actually price a fixed mortgage off, jumped from 3.33% to 3.60% in under a week, as Robert McLister noted in the Financial Post on November 16. Buying power got tighter after the October deals were already written.

Confidence was not exactly roaring into that. The Bloomberg-Nanos Canadian Confidence Index was 50.98 for the four weeks ending October 30, below its long-term average of 54.65. The expectations index, which includes the outlook for the economy and property prices, sat at 47.77. Nik Nanos called it the slow lane. A presale buyer is being asked to commit years out, with their home equity worth less and their fixed rate already moving. Rental is holding up because its financing does not depend on those retail buyers in the same way. That is a real offset. It does not replace the ownership units a turned cycle will need.

Chart: Active residential listings, Ontario vs Quebec. Daniel Foch via homiesai.com/stats. Data: CREA.

What it means

For builders: Quebec still has rising benchmarks and a ratio in balanced territory, which is the kind of comparable set that can support a presale. Ontario does not, and October's rate move does not help. I would not plan a national absorption number as if the demand problem stopped at the GTA border.

For policymakers: Ontario's resale "balance" is not proof the supply problem is solved. Sellers stopped listing. Builders stopped starting. Both are rational. Together they set up the next shortage. National inventory is about 197,000 listings, a little above CREA's long-term average of 190,000, with five months of supply. On paper, Canada looks balanced. Underneath, the biggest province is balancing by doing less, and the sales weakness that started in Toronto and Vancouver is no longer staying there. If we "solve" a glut by starting fewer homes, what does 2029 look like? The monthly CREA release will not answer that. The starts number might.

items.title: Housing market ‘headed into hibernation’ after quiet October
items.description: National sales and prices barely budge as buyers stay on the sidelines
items.content: <p>National sales and prices barely budge as buyers stay on the sidelines</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639305304352006566.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: National sales and prices barely budge as buyers stay on the sidelines
items.body:
Canadian home sales stayed essentially flat in October as rising interest rates and economic uncertainty kept potential buyers in a wait-and-see pattern.

New Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data showed the number of sales recorded last month inched 0.3% higher compared with September, while average prices barely budged on a month-over-month basis.

The latest data reflects a national market that’s still struggling to gather pace as tariff turmoil and higher fuel prices spurred by the US-Iran war continue to stir concern about the economic outlook.

Michael Davenport, senior economist at Oxford Economics, suggested the market would remain subdued for the remainder of the year. “Canada’s resale housing market had a quiet October, and we think it’s headed into hibernation for the winter,” he said in a statement after the release.

“Home sales and prices edged up last month, but that only partially offset declines in September, and may reflect some buyers with preapproved mortgage rates and others pulling forward purchases ahead of expected Bank of Canada rate hikes.”

CREA economist: Don’t expect a flurry of big BoC hikes

The Bank of Canada stepped off the sidelines at the end of October, announcing its first interest rate hike for more than three years in a fresh blow to affordability.

Still, CREA senior economist Shaun Cathcart said homebuyers shouldn’t expect a similar series of raises to the BoC’s last rate-hiking cycle, when it spiked its benchmark rate by a total of 475 basis points in 2022 and 2023 in a bid to combat rampant inflation.

“With the Bank’s preferred inflation measures still very well behaved, this is unlikely to be a repeat of the 2022 tightening cycle,” Cathcart said in remarks accompanying CREA’s latest release. “Rather, it is more likely to be of the mild to moderate variety, although that distinction does carry extra weight in times of stretched affordability.”

New listings also moved slightly higher in October, increasing by 0.8% over the previous month. But CREA chair Garry Bhaura said the market outlook is still better than many would have expected when mortgage rates began to climb after the summer.

“Despite most forecasters sharpening their pencils and lowering their predictions, so far we’ve only seen a slight slowdown in housing activity from the summer to the fall, probably less than many would have predicted in an environment of rising interest rates,” he said.

Seasonally adjusted October sales came in at 446,100, while the aggregate composite MLS home price index (HPI) was $656,200 for the month. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, the national average price was $678,584 – a drop of 1.6% compared with October 2025.

Government action could help, but BoC may move again in December

Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper pointed to the federal government’s proposed adjustment to the foreign buyer ban to exclude new home purchases as a step that could boost the national housing market moving into 2027.

But Davenport said he doesn’t expect the BoC to move back to a holding pattern next month. “Rising mortgage rates, a soft labour market, and elevated job insecurity from the trade war with the US will likely cause housing demand to weaken in the near term, pushing home sales and prices modestly lower before a tepid recovery gets underway next spring,” he said.

“We don’t expect the recent softness in the housing market to deter the BoC from hiking another 25 [basis points] to 2.75% in December.”
